paper.title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
paper.note: Full 2026/27 TMS/AIS/MRP paper — self-contained (not a covering report). Companion papers on the 10 February 2026 Cabinet agenda were the Capital Strategy and Capital Programme (s259659, s259660) and the Q2 Budget Monitoring Update (s259622); this TMS paper carries its own capital-expenditure table (3.2.1), CFR projections (3.2.2), portfolio position (6.1.1), prudential indicators (Appendix 1), MRP policy (Section 5) and Annual Investment Strategy (Section 7) — enough to work from without opening the companions. Contact officer front sheet gives Lorna Soufian, CSS Treasury Manager, lorna.soufian@stockport.gov.uk — sole address published in the paper. S151 named on the summary sheet as Jonathan Davies, Director of Finance (sign-off block 5.1 spells 'Johnathan Davies' — inconsistency in the paper itself; no email address published). Meeting dates have passed by six months; email is drafted to land ahead of the autumn mid-year report cycle.

facts.note: Includes £13.7m of OLTL (finance-leases/similar) inside CFR total per 3.2.2 narrative. Non-HRA CFR falls each year because MRP (£33.268m in 26/27) outpaces new financing (£55.450m borrowing requirement); HRA CFR rises because HRA borrowing (£22.388m in 27/28) is not matched by MRP (nil, per 5.8 — HRA basic MRP is nil under former reg 28/29 SI 2003/3146).

Under-borrowing wedge from balance-sheet identity: £80.152m (forecast 31.03.26) → £47.084m (26/27) → £15.527m (27/28) → over-borrowed £11.138m by 28/29.

We expect to externalise a portion of our internal debt.' Under-borrowing shrinks from £80.152m to £15.527m across the MTFS as the £152.732m 2026/27 capital programme (including £100m recyclable equity/loan facility for the MDC town-centre delivery strategy) pushes external debt up faster than CFR.

facts.value: £100m of PWLB at average 4.73% maturing between June and November 2026, from the £187m secured in early 2025

source.table: paragraph 6.4.5, Proactive Refinancing and Risk Mitigation

facts.note: The single biggest treasury decision the council will take in 2026/27. Companion £87m tranche at 4.87% matures 2027/28. Paper's own words: 'Our immediate focus for 2026 is the seamless refinancing of the £100m maturing tranche.' Preferred routes at 6.4.6: LA-to-LA market or short-dated PWLB, 'as rates at the shorter end of the curve (under 5 years) are currently more attractive than long-term rates.' Our file at 2026-08-16 holds 8 loans in the under-12-months bucket totalling £92.5m at weighted 4.72% — matches the paper's shape to ~1bp on rate, with the £7.5m gap likely accounted for by loans already matured through summer 2026.

source.table: paragraph 6.4.10, PWLB Borrowing Triggers

facts.note: Dated and falsifiable. Certainty-rate basis — HRA rate 40bp lower. Triggers sit exactly at MUFG's own forecast rates for each quarter (compare 6.3.2 forecast table with 6.4.10 trigger table) — construction means Stockport will only draw at rates the forecaster already says are imminent. Not raised in the email because it reads as pointed criticism in a first cold approach.

source.table: paragraph 6.4.11, Forward Target Borrowing Rates

facts.note: Explicit forward view — 'In alignment with our strategy to delay long-term commitments until rates fall, we have established forward target borrowing rates predicated on market expectations for the end of Q4 2027, when rates are anticipated to be more favourable.' Dated (Q4 2027), specific (four maturities, precise rates), falsifiable. Ranks alongside NEL's 'two quarter-point cuts to 3.25% by end of 2026' as the strongest kind of hook.

facts.value: 'Our long-term neutral Bank Rate target remains 3.50%'

facts.note: 'current PWLB rates remain above this level. We will only move toward long-term fixed-rate borrowing if market certainty becomes a higher priority than immediate cost savings.' Explicit trigger for switching from short-dated to long-dated borrowing. Only a handful of the papers we've read commit to such a specific neutral-rate anchor.

source.table: paragraph 4.2.1, Estimates of the Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream

facts.note: HRA ratio rises 2.55 percentage points over two years while HRA CFR only grows 15% (£163.759m → £188.000m per 3.2.2) — implies HRA revenue base is projected to flatten or shrink. summary.text:
Stockport's 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and MRP Policy, approved by Cabinet on 10 February 2026 and Council on 26 February 2026, is a self-contained treasury paper (not a covering report) with all tables, rates and projections in the body. Coming to you six months on because the £100m refinancing the paper flags in paragraph 6.4.5 is now half-way through its window.

The refinancing story is the hook. Paragraph 6.4.5 sets it out: £100m of PWLB at an average 4.73% matures between June and November 2026, drawn from the £187m the council secured in early 2025 during 'a period of short-term market illiquidity' and split into two tranches to manage refinancing risk (the second, £87m at 4.87%, matures in 2027/28). Our file for Stockport at 2026-08-16 holds 8 loans in the under-12-months bucket totalling £92.5m at a weighted 4.72% — matches the shape of that £100m tranche to ~1bp on rate, with a small principal gap consistent with loans already run off through the summer. Paragraph 6.4.6 sets the preferred routes: LA-to-LA or short-dated PWLB, 'as rates at the shorter end of the curve (under 5 years) are currently more attractive than long-term rates'.

The paper is unusually specific in the numbers it publishes forward. Paragraph 6.4.10 sets quarter-by-quarter PWLB borrowing triggers (5y 4.10%, 10y 4.80%, 25y 5.50%, 50y 5.30% for Q4 on certainty rates); paragraph 6.4.11 goes further and sets forward target rates for end-Q4 2027 (5y 4.10%, 10y 4.70%, 25y 5.30%, 50y 5.10%). Both are dated and falsifiable against the daily curve. Neutral Bank Rate anchor stated explicitly at 6.4.6 as 3.50%. Balance-sheet identity ties every year to £1k across four years of the MTFS (£80.152m → £47.084m → £15.527m → over-borrowed £11.138m under-borrowing wedge, on the paper's own 6.1.1 table); CFR rollforward ties every year on both non-HRA and HRA — as clean an arithmetic tie as we've had.

Loan-book reconciliation is not possible from this paper. Paper prints Gross Borrowing £843.800m at 31.03.26 forecast (6.1.1) as a single line covering PWLB + LOBO + market + short-term LA, with no PWLB-specific sub-total. Our file at 2026-03-31 holds 46 PWLB loans totalling £602,704,989 at weighted 3.8352%; the residual £241m sits in the £7.5m LOBO (6.5.3) plus short-term and other market debt. Data-side observation logged for owner attention: price_book.py returns empty at 2025-03-31 for Stockport, suggesting our file capture starts at or after the £187m early-2025 draw. Per PIPELINE convention the loan-book claim and the reconciliation gap are recorded here in the note but NOT quoted in the email; the tranche-shape match at the under-12-months bucket is cited qualitatively instead.

Other points logged. HRA financing-cost ratio steps 8.91% → 9.52% → 11.46% across the MTFS while HRA CFR only grows 15% — a real strain on the HRA revenue base worth naming (4.2.1). Previously Supported GF Borrowing £137.988m at 1.4.2026 amortises straight-line to 31.3.2065 at £3.538m annually — 39 more years of fixed £138m committed MRP before any new MRP on the 26/27 capital programme (5.4.3); arithmetic ties to the paper's own end-date exactly. Annuity-method MRP anchored to prevailing PWLB rates (5.4.1) — same shape as Tower Hamlets, Derbyshire, Rutland; not led on because the paper carries stronger hooks. LOBO exposure just £7.5m with semi-annual options (6.5.3), material because in 2016/17-2017/18 Stockport converted £60m of Barclays and RBS LOBOs to vanilla long-term (6.5.12) — well ahead of the LOBO-call wave now moving through the sector. Trigger table at 6.4.10 sits at exactly MUFG's own forecast rates for each quarter (compare with 6.3.2) — construction defensible but reads as 'borrow at rates the forecaster says are already imminent'; flagged internal-only, not raised.

officer.subject: Your £100m 4.73% tranche is refinancing now — and the triggers you set for it
officer.body:
Dear Lorna,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. More — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a few thoughts on your 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that Cabinet approved on 10 February and Council on 26 February — coming to you now because the refinancing you flag in paragraph 6.4.5 is half-way through its window. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's nothing being sold. The paper is unusually specific in the rates it publishes forward, which is what makes it worth writing about.

On the £100m tranche. Paragraph 6.4.5 sets it out: £100m of PWLB at an average 4.73% maturing between June and November 2026, from the £187m the council secured in early 2025. Our file for Stockport shows a cluster of 8 loans in the under-12-months bucket totalling £92.5m at a weighted 4.72% — the shape matches what the paper describes, with a small amount already run off through the summer. Where those loans land against the curve at the moments they roll is the number the outturn will turn on, and paragraph 6.4.6 sets the first-look preference clearly: LA-to-LA or short-dated PWLB, because 'rates at the shorter end of the curve (under 5 years) are currently more attractive than long-term rates.'

Two other features of the paper that are unusually explicit. Paragraph 6.4.10 publishes quarter-by-quarter PWLB borrowing triggers — for Q4, 5-year 4.10%, 10-year 4.80%, 25-year 5.50%, 50-year 5.30% (certainty rates). Paragraph 6.4.11 goes further and sets forward target rates for end-Q4 2027: 5-year 4.10%, 10-year 4.70%, 25-year 5.30%, 50-year 5.10%. Both are dated and testable against the daily curve. We publish the certainty-rate curve at both fixings at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — for a team running against explicit triggers, having the trigger and the market on the same screen each morning is the useful thing.

Paragraph 4.2.1 is worth its own line. Your HRA financing-cost ratio moves from 8.91% in 2026/27 to 9.52% in 2027/28 to 11.46% in 2028/29 — 2.55 percentage points over two years — while HRA CFR only grows about 15% across that window (£163.759m to £188.000m per 3.2.2). That's the HRA borrowing programme working through against a flatter revenue base. Not a criticism; it's just what the figures do, and it's the kind of step that scrutiny may want a line on.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway is becoming central to how strategies are framed. Your chart at 3.2.4 shows an existing loan-debt line sitting around £430-500m through the 2030s and 2040s from an £850m starting point — a long tail. Our interactive version tied to daily rate feeds is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, useful once the CIPFA changes land.

Three of the academy courses fit Stockport's shape. Reading the PWLB certainty curve is the mechanics behind your trigger table at 6.4.10. Refinancing tactics on short-dated PWLB speaks to the £100m you're rolling now. Liability Benchmark in practice ties to the pathway you plot at 3.2.4. All courses are free to local authorities until end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts on the platform give the finance team access to the daily data and the archive.

And if you find it useful, mentioning it to colleagues would help us more than anything. We're small — word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy, Cabinet 10 February 2026 (doc s259662), at https://democracy.stockport.gov.uk/documents/s259662/2026-27-treasury-management-strategy-annual-investment-strat.pdf.

Not raised in the email as a cross-check — chosen instead to lead on the refinancing story and the explicit triggers, per the hook-selection rule of drafting from the council's position, not from whichever tool ran cleanest.
reconciliation.cfr_rollforward: Ties every year on both non-HRA and HRA across the MTFS.
reconciliation.mrp_legacy: £137.988m / £3.538m = 39.00 years remaining; end-point 31.3.2065 ties exactly to paper (5.4.3).

cross_council_observations.trigger_publication: Very few of the 77 councils read so far publish quarter-by-quarter borrowing triggers on this level of specificity — Middlesbrough's 4.75% single trigger is the closest we have. Draft names it as a feature of Stockport's paper without cross-referring.
cross_council_observations.forward_target_rates: Rarer still — dated forward rates for a specific quarter (Q4 2027) two years out. Draft names it without comparing.
cross_council_observations.mrp_annuity_pwlb_rate: Stockport joins Tower Hamlets, Derbyshire, Rutland in anchoring the annuity-method MRP to the prevailing PWLB rate — not led on because the refinancing and trigger hooks are stronger, but latent for any follow-up.
cross_council_observations.lobo_conversion_history: £60m of Barclays and RBS LOBOs converted to vanilla long-term loans in 2016/17-2017/18 — well ahead of the LOBO-call wave (Dexia at Kent, Tameside; Newcastle; York; Bath & NE Somerset) now moving through the sector. Not raised because it is 8-9 years old and reads as history.

officer.voice: Russell Tew, first-person. Not templated: no bold headers, no bulleted summary, contractions throughout. Leads with the refinancing tranche that is half-way through its window (the strongest single hook), then the trigger and forward-target rates (dated and falsifiable — the second-strongest hook), then the HRA financing-cost step (a real observation from their own indicator table), then the standing liability-benchmark pathway inclusion, then targeted courses. Deliberately no numerical rate-move claim — no reliable current PWLB curve to cite at the point of drafting. Deliberately no aggregate loan-book claim — paper does not publish a PWLB total to reconcile against.
